1.s: “I have loved you,” says God, but the people ask, “How have you loved us?” Priests offer blind and sick animals; God’s name will be great among the nations.
1.d: Malachi’s sermons use a form called disputation, a structured argument; the first states that God loves Israel [[tosn:Malachi 1:2–5]]. “Loved” and “hated” are covenant words for choosing and separation [[tosn:Malachi 1:2]] [[tosn:Malachi 1:3]]. Paul quotes 1:2–3 in Romans 9:13 [[bible:Romans 9:13]].

2.s: God rebukes priests who cause many to stumble, and husbands who break faith with the wife of their youth: “One who hates and divorces… covers his garment with violence!”
2.d: The priests were to teach God’s law and guard his covenant [[tosn:Malachi 2:7]]. The third message calls divorce a betrayal: the people broke faith with God and with their wives [[tosn:Malachi 2:10]] [[tosn:Malachi 2:10–16]].

3.s: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me.” The Lord will come suddenly to his temple like a refiner’s fire. “Bring the whole tithe… test me now in this.”
3.d: “My messenger” (mal’aki) plays on Malachi’s name; Jesus applied this verse to John the Baptist [[tosn:Malachi 3:1]] [[bible:Matthew 11:10]]. Poor tithes meant the nation was robbing God (3:8–12) [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]].

4.s: The day is coming, burning like a furnace, but “to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings.” “I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day.”
4.d: The book closes with Moses, standing for the Law, and Elijah, for the Prophets [[tosn:Malachi 4:4–6]]. The New Testament identifies John the Baptist with the promised Elijah [[tosn:Malachi 4:5–6]] [[bible:Matthew 11:14]].
